name: Lead-based ceruse

card.summary: A historical lead-based white face paste that whitened skin and poisoned its users.
card.note: Contains lead; documented to cause lead poisoning.

quick.overview:
Ceruse was a white paste made from lead, used from antiquity to the 18th century to give a pale complexion and cover blemishes. Venetian ceruse was the most prized version.

It is a historical practice rather than a current product, documented here because it is a well-known example of a lightening agent with serious harms.
quick.mechanism: The paste was applied to the face as an opaque white cover, with lead-containing pigment suspended in vinegar or similar carriers. It masked skin tone rather than altering melanin.
quick.risks: Historical accounts describe lead poisoning from skin absorption, with abdominal pain, organ damage, convulsions and death, plus skin damage that led to heavier application. The WHO lists lead as a major cosmetic chemical of concern.

lead: Ceruse, also called Venetian ceruse, Venetian white or white lead, was a cosmetic paste of lead carbonate used for centuries to whiten the face and cover blemishes, scars and freckles. Mixed with water and vinegar, it formed a paste that adhered well to the skin, and its opacity concealed imperfections, giving the smooth, pale complexion that late medieval and Renaissance beauty ideals favoured.[1] Pale skin signalled wealth and leisure in the societies that used it, since outdoor labourers tanned.[1]

The main ingredient was basic lead carbonate (2PbCO3.Pb(OH)2), related to the mineral cerussite. A 16th-century method used lead sheets and vinegar in sealed clay pots left for several weeks, so that lead acetate formed and then turned into lead carbonate on exposure to air. Italy exported ceruse from the 14th century, and the Venetian product was regarded as the finest, selling for up to twice the price of ordinary lead white; counterfeit versions reportedly added chalk or whiting.[1]

Repeated application allowed lead to be absorbed through the skin, and historical accounts describe poisoning, skin damage, organ damage and death among users.[1] Lead is not a legitimate cosmetic ingredient today; the World Health Organization listed lead as one of ten major chemicals of concern in cosmetics in 2010.[1]

angle.text: Ceruse worked as a heavy opaque foundation that whitened the face and hid scars, freckles and blemishes. It is documented here as a historical product whose lead content caused harm.

paras: Lead-based whitening is described as beginning in ancient Rome, where the product was called cerussa, with similar white cosmetics in Egypt and Greece.[1] Late medieval and early Renaissance ideals favoured a pale complexion with red cheeks and lips.[1] Surgeons also used ceruse to dry moist sores.[1]

From the 14th-century Italy, especially Venice, exported ceruse, and the Venetian product was regarded as the finest and sold at a premium.[1] A 1688 recipe described ceruse as water, vinegar and lead.[1]

Elizabeth I of England is widely thought to have used it, possibly after a smallpox scar in 1562, though some historians, including Anna Riehl and Kate Maltby, argue there is little evidence for this.[1] Isabella d'Este was a devoted user and was described by Pietro Aretino in 1534 as heavily made up, and Maria Coventry, Countess of Coventry, who died in 1760 aged 27, is believed to have died of lead poisoning, earning the nickname "Death by Vanity".[1] Some royal men also reportedly used it, since pale skin signalled that one did not work outdoors.[1]

Makeup was viewed with suspicion in many periods: women who wore it were often seen as promiscuous or unfaithful, and the Latin word fucus, meaning false colour, reflected the view that makeup was unnatural.[1] Pale skin signified wealth and nobility, according to Wikipedia's article, rather than race.[1]

Accounts describe abdominal pain, paralysis, convulsions, nausea, high blood pressure, reduced fertility and confusion from lead absorbed through the skin.[1] The paste could also mottle, peel and scar the skin, which led users to apply further layers, producing a cycle of dependence.[1] Hair loss at the hairline may have helped shape the fashion for high foreheads.[1] Scientific studies confirmed lead's dangers only at the end of the 18th century, and users often knew of the risks but continued.[1]

Modern medical references describe lead poisoning in adults as causing early nonspecific symptoms such as fatigue, abdominal pain and mood change, and with chronic exposure kidney damage, cardiovascular disease, nervous system effects and reduced sperm count.[2] Wikipedia's lead poisoning article also names kohl, an ancient cosmetic from the Middle East, South Asia and parts of Africa, as a source of lead in cosmetics.[2]
